owner_hypothesis: It is my personal opinion that the slavery today is worse than it was a hundred years ago.
question: Which forms of coercive labor, financial incentives and legal institutions persisted or changed, and can comparable data establish a worsening from approximately 1926 to the present?
conclusion: Economic exploitation and coercion persist, and selected institutional continuities are documented. The recovered data support a rise in global estimated forced labour between 2016 and 2021. They do not provide comparable U.S. or global measures for 1926 and 2026 sufficient to establish the broader century-long claim. Legal abolition and subsequent protections are material changes; implementation and enforcement must be assessed separately.

evidence.title: U.S. chattel slavery population baseline
evidence.population: United States census population, as reported by the Census Bureau
evidence.finding: The census enumerated legal chattel slavery. This is a U.S. count from 166 years before the review, not the requested 1926 baseline.

sources.title: Census Bureau, Abraham Lincoln and the census

evidence.title: Abolition with a punishment exception
evidence.finding: Ratification abolished slavery and involuntary servitude while retaining a criminal-punishment exception. This changed legal status; the exception and subsequent penal institutions require their own review.

evidence.title: Money paid to institutions for prison labor in the 1923 survey
evidence.payer: Contractors using contract and piece-price systems in surveyed state and federal prisons
evidence.currency: nominal USD for one reported fiscal year per institution; fiscal-year endings differ in the 1922/1923 survey periods
evidence.finding: BLS reported $3,290,777 paid to institutions for the labor of 9,660 prisoners under contract and piece-price systems: approximately $340.66 per prisoner per year. These are institutional receipts, not prisoner wages. The 104-institution survey covered one full fiscal year for each institution, with differing year-end dates in 1922/1923; it was not one common calendar-year national census. Juvenile, county, city and military institutions were generally excluded, subject to the report's stated exceptions. The reported receipt excludes some overtask bonuses paid directly to prisoners.
evidence.policy_relation: Documents a legally structured labor market and state financial incentive; not a demonstrated bribe or a national modern-slavery count.

sources.title: BLS Bulletin 372, Convict Labor in 1923
sources.locator: Printed pages 2–3, Introduction; original published January 1925; searchable transcription is OCR

evidence.title: Documented post-emancipation institutional continuity
evidence.finding: The Library of Congress describes how criminalization, arrests and fees supplied convict leasing after emancipation. This supports a specific institutional connection to coercive labor, rather than an inference from a present person's ancestors or school history.
evidence.evidence_kind: Institutional historical synthesis with archival links, not an original transaction ledger

sources.title: Library of Congress, The Convict Leasing System
sources.locator: June 17, 2021 article body, excluding reader comments

evidence.title: Global forced labour and forced marriage estimates
evidence.finding: ILO, Walk Free and IOM estimate 49.6 million people in modern slavery in 2021: 27.6 million in forced labour and 22 million in forced marriage. Global 2016–2021 comparisons are supported with methodological qualifications; finer comparisons have additional limits. These are not a 2026 count, a U.S. census or a measure of ordinary employment, debt or inequality.

sources.title: Global Estimates of Modern Slavery, 2022
sources.locator: Printed pages 20–22 and methodological annex pages 109–113; PDF hosting date does not change observation year

evidence.title: Profits from coercive labor
evidence.finding: ILO estimates private-economy forced-labour profits; the 2014 comparison is inflation-adjusted. This is an estimate of exploitation proceeds, not lobbying expenditure, corporate revenue or profit attributable to the AI companies in this study.

sources.title: ILO, Annual profits from forced labour
sources.locator: March 19, 2024, global profit and inflation-adjusted comparison paragraphs

evidence.title: Trade law changed its treatment of forced-labor imports
evidence.finding: The Trade Facilitation and Trade Enforcement Act removed the consumptive-demand exception to the Tariff Act's forced-labor import prohibition. This is evidence of a legal change, not evidence that forced-labor goods ceased entering supply chains or that a particular donor bought the change.

sources.title: CRS, Forced Labor Trafficking in the International Fishing Sector
sources.locator: February 29, 2016, Recent Trade and Customs Legislation

comparison_rules: Compare like geography, population, legal/economic definition, observation year and measurement method before comparing counts or rates.
Do not divide a present global estimate by an historical U.S. count and call the result a change in slavery.
Treat the severity of harm, prevalence, total people affected, legal status and profits as separate dimensions. No universal worse score is calculated.

Use public biography, adult roles and speeches only to establish a documented connection. Childhood, shared ancestry and institutional membership do not by themselves establish motives, coordinated action or culpability.
Historical oppression and present exploitation can be established without asserting that all people in a racial, religious or economic group share guilt.
missing_for_century_comparison: Comparable 1926 and 2026 U.S. prevalence data under one definition
Comparable geographic coverage and estimates of undercount
A declared measure of severity and supporting data
Company-specific contracts, suppliers, enforcement findings or adjudications before assigning modern forced-labor responsibility
